props.title: Prospero's Books
props.initialSlug: Shakespeare's Tempest reimagined in surreal splendor

sections.content: Peter Greenaway's avant-garde masterpiece Prospero's Books revolutionized Shakespeare adaptation through groundbreaking digital effects and layered imagery. John Gielgud's commanding performance as Prospero merges with Greenaway's signature visual excess - multiple frames, text overlays, and nude choreography create a hypnotic dreamscape. This radical approach connects to other experimental Shakespeare films like Throne of Blood (1957) and Titus (1999), but pushes further into pure cinematic art.

sections.content: Greenaway's obsession with cataloging and categorization manifests in the 24 magical books that structure the film. Each tome gets lavish treatment through pioneering HD video effects from Paintbox - technology that influenced later digital experimentation in films like The Pillow Book (1996) and Russian Ark (2002). The books themselves become characters, with elaborate animated sequences showing their contents spilling across the frame.

The film's treatment of Shakespeare's language is revolutionary. Rather than traditional dialogue scenes, Prospero speaks all parts while we see the other characters in motion. This technique, combined with multiple image layers and constant visual transformation, creates a uniquely cinematic interpretation that influenced later experimental adaptations like Romeo + Juliet (1996) and Macbeth (2015). SUBHEAD: Visual Innovation and Digital Pioneers

Prospero's Books marked one of the first major uses of high-definition video and digital effects in art cinema. Greenaway worked with painter Tom Phillips to create elaborate visual palimpsests - layering text, classical paintings, and live action in ways that predicted today's complex digital compositions. This pioneering work opened doors for later digital experimenters like The Cell (2000) and What Dreams May Come (1998).
